pages.title: Broadcasting in NumPy
pages.content:
Imagine you have a dataset containing the heights of different people in meters, and you need to convert all these heights to centimeters. This operation requires multiplying each height by 100.

Broadcasting describes how NumPy treats arrays with different shapes during arithmetic operations. Subject to certain constraints, the smaller array is "broadcast" across the larger array so that they have compatible shapes.

We will learn the following in this topic
- Broadcasting in 1D arrays
- Rules of broadcasting
- Broadcasting with multi-dimensional arrays
- Practice problems / debugging exercises to help reinforce our understanding

pages.title: Broadcasting arrays of different sizes
pages.content:
In the previous problem, when multiplying sales by growth_factors, NumPy applies broadcasting.
- growth_factors has a shape of (3,) (it is a 1-dimensional array with 3 elements).
- sales has a shape of (3, 1) (it is a 2-dimensional array with 3 rows and 1 column).

NumPy "stretches" the growth_factors array to match the shape of sales:
```python
growth_factors = np.array([[1.1, 1.2, 1.3],
                           [1.1, 1.2, 1.3],
                           [1.1, 1.2, 1.3]])
```

Now, the two arrays have compatible shapes, and NumPy can perform element-wise multiplication:
```python
forecasted_sales = sales * growth_factors
```

The resulting forecasted_sales array is
```python
[[11. 12. 13.]
 [22. 24. 26.]
 [33. 36. 39.]]
```

practiceProblems.title: Broadcasting rules
practiceProblems.description:
- Rule 1: If the arrays do not have the same rank, prepend the shape of the smaller array with ones until both shapes have the same length.
- Rule 2: The size in each dimension of the output shape is the maximum size in that dimension of the input shapes.
- Rule 3: An array can be broadcast across another array only if the size of the dimension in the array is 1 or matches the size of the dimension in the other array.

Let us understand these rules again with an example - check out the code in the IDE - click on Submit to see the result.
- Dimensions of Arrays:
   - matrix is a 3x3 array (shape = (3, 3)).
   - vector is a 1D array with 3 elements (shape = (3,))
- According to NumPy broadcasting rules, when operating on arrays of different shapes, NumPy compares their shapes element-wise starting from the trailing dimensions.
   - vector is broadcasted to match the shape of matrix. Thus vector becomes `[[1 0 -1]
 [1 0 -1]
 [1 0 -1]]`
- Element-wise addition is then performed

practiceProblems.title: Matrix multiplication and Inversion
practiceProblems.description:
Let us now review the syntax of matrix multiplication using NumPy - check out the code given in the IDE.

A similar concept to matrix multiplication is matrix inversion - matrix inversion finds a matrix that, when multiplied with the original matrix, yields the identity matrix. Only square matrices can be inverted. 
An identity matrix is a special kind of square matrix that has ones on the main diagonal (from the top left to the bottom right) and zeros in all other positions. 
```python
[[ 1 0 0]
 [ 0 1 0]
 [ 0 0 1]]
```
Check out the code given in the IDE where we compute the inverse matrix - also note that when the inverse is multiplied with the original matrix, we get the identity matrix.

practiceProblems.title: Matrix transposition
practiceProblems.description:
The transpose of a matrix flips it over its diagonal, switching rows and columns.

Consider the following example
```python
matrix_a = np.array([[1], [2], [3]] )
print(matrix_a)
print(np.transpose(matrix_a))
```
The above code gives us the output
```python
[[1]
 [2]
 [3]]
[[1 2 3]]
```
The original matrix has 3 rows and 1 column - the transpose has 1 row and 3 columns.

### Task
You are given a 2 x 3 matrix. Use the transpose function and output the result to the console.

practiceProblems.title: Solve linear equations using matrices
practiceProblems.description:
Linear equations often arise in real-world scenarios, such as physics, engineering, economics, and more. Matrices provide an efficient way to solve systems of linear equations, especially when dealing with multiple variables.

Suppose we have the following system of linear equations representing a real-world problem, such as determining the quantities of ingredients needed in a recipe, balancing chemical equations, or analyzing electrical circuits:	​  
 2x + y − z = 8 \
−3x − y + 2z = −11 \
−2x + y + 2z = −3 \
​
### Steps to Solve Using Matrices:
- Represent the System as a Matrix Equation\
The system of linear equations can be written in the form $A \cdot X = B$
```python
A = [[2, 1, -1]
     [-3, -1, 2]
     [-2, 1, 2]]

X = [[x]
     [y]
     [z]]

B = [[8]
     [-11]
     [-3]]
```
- Find the Solution\
To solve for X, we use the equation $X = A^{-1} \cdot B$ where $A^{-1}$ is the inverse of matrix A.

Check out implementation of the above solution in the IDE.

practiceProblems.title: Unique elements
practiceProblems.description:
np.unique function returns the sorted unique elements of an array.
```python
campaign_a = np.array([1, 1, 3, 4, 3, 6])
print(np.unique(campaign_a))      # Output - [1 3 4 6]
```

How does this work in 2D arrays? \
Imagine you are analyzing survey data from different groups of participants where each group provides responses to multiple questions. You want to find unique responses across all groups for a particular question.

Consider a 2D array survey_responses where each row represents responses from different groups and each column represents responses to different questions.

In this example:
- survey_responses is a 2D array where each row corresponds to responses from a different group.
- We extract responses to a specific question (question 2 in this case) using slicing (survey_responses[:, 1]).
- np.unique function is used to find unique responses to question 2 across all groups.

Check out this code in the IDE.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
np.unique function returns the sorted unique elements of an array.
```python
campaign_a = np.array([1, 1, 3, 4, 3, 6])
print(np.unique(campaign_a))      # Output - [1 3 4 6]
```

How does this work in 2D arrays? \
Imagine you are analyzing survey data from different groups of participants where each group provides responses to multiple questions. You want to find unique responses across all groups for a particular question.

Consider a 2D array survey_responses where each row represents responses from different groups and each column represents responses to different questions.

In this example:
- survey_responses is a 2D array where each row corresponds to responses from a different group.
- We extract responses to a specific question (question 2 in this case) using slicing (survey_responses[:, 1]).
- np.unique function is used to find unique responses to question 2 across all groups.

practiceProblems.title: Intersection and Union
practiceProblems.description:
Let us look at our previous example again - Imagine you have two lists of customer IDs from two different marketing campaigns. You want to find out:
- Which customers participated in both campaigns.
- Which customers are unique to each campaign.

np.intersect1d function returns the sorted, unique values that are in both of the input arrays.

np.union1d function returns the sorted, unique values that are in either of the input arrays.

np.setdiff1d function returns the sorted, unique values in array1 that are not in array2.
